title: Is one more loaf free?
hook: Your $20 is spent to the last cent. Add one more loaf: what has to go back?

knows: that a budget is a fixed amount to spend
doesNotKnow: that a budget turns every purchase into a trade against another
that the trade-off between two goods is the ratio of their prices

misconception: Buying one more of something is free if it is still within budget.
objective: The learner can explain that inside a fixed budget every extra unit of one good costs a fixed number of units of another, equal to the price ratio.

claims.text: With $20, apples at $2 and loaves at $4, a cart of 3 loaves leaves $8, which buys at most 4 apples; adding a fourth loaf leaves $4, room for only 2 apples, so 2 apples are pushed out.
Each loaf takes the room of 2 apples, because $4 / $2 = 2; once the money is all spent, one more loaf means 2 fewer apples.
claims.source: Price ratio 4 / 2 = 2; maxApples(l) = (20 - 4l) / 2 = 10 - 2l falls by 2 per loaf.

claims.text: Inside a fixed budget, one more of one good means giving up some of another; the trade-off is the ratio of the prices.
claims.source: Budget constraint: the slope of the budget line is the relative price (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 21 'The Theory of Consumer Choice', section 'The Budget Constraint').

claims.text: The prices are made up for the example.
claims.source: Stage chip 'made-up prices'; reveal's last line.

recall.question: You have $30 to spend on movie tickets at $10 and snacks at $5. If you add one more ticket, how many snacks must you give up?
recall.why: Inside a fixed budget a $10 ticket takes the room of two $5 snacks. The trade-off is the price ratio, 10 / 5 = 2.
